lesson.title: From Idea to Voltage: What a Signal Actually Is
lesson.summary: A signal is the physical, changing quantity, a voltage, a light pulse, a radio wave, that actually carries data across a communication link.
lesson.body:
A signal is a physical quantity that varies over time in a way that carries information. It might be a voltage that rises and falls on a copper wire, a beam of light that switches on and off inside a fiber optic cable, or a radio wave whose strength changes in the air. Whatever form it takes, a signal is how data actually travels across a communication link, because data by itself, as an abstract collection of bits, cannot move anywhere without being turned into something physical first.

A simple example makes this concrete. A traditional landline telephone takes the sound of your voice, a wave of continuously changing air pressure, and uses a microphone to convert it into a continuously changing electrical voltage. That voltage waveform is the signal. It travels down the copper telephone wire to the other end, where a speaker converts the voltage back into sound waves that the person on the other end hears. Nothing about your voice itself moved down the wire, only the electrical signal that represented it.

Signals are described using a few basic properties. Amplitude is the strength or size of the signal at a given moment, such as how high a voltage rises. Frequency is how quickly the signal repeats a pattern, measured in cycles per second, or hertz. A signal that completes 1,000 full cycles every second has a frequency of 1,000 hertz, usually written as 1 kilohertz. Frequency and period are opposites of each other: the period is the time one cycle takes, so a 1 kilohertz signal has a period of 1 divided by 1,000, or 0.001 seconds, which is 1 millisecond per cycle. These properties matter because the equipment on both ends of a link has to agree on how information is encoded into changes in amplitude, frequency, or timing.

Every communication link, no matter what physical medium it uses, ultimately depends on some kind of signal. Ethernet cables carry electrical voltage signals. Fiber optic cables carry pulses of light. Wi-Fi and cellular networks carry radio wave signals through the air. The medium changes, but the underlying job of the signal stays the same: represent information as a physical, measurable variation that a receiver on the other end can detect and interpret. A signal also tends to weaken as it travels, an effect called attenuation, and it can pick up unwanted noise from nearby electrical activity or interference along the way, which is why network equipment sometimes needs to boost or clean up a signal partway along a long cable run.

Signals generally fall into one of two broad categories, based on how they represent that variation. The next two chapters look at each in turn: analog signals, which vary smoothly and continuously, and digital signals, which take on only a small, fixed set of distinct values. That distinction turns out to matter enormously for how much noise a signal can tolerate and how far it can travel before the information it carries starts to degrade.
